thesis: This paper argues that making disciples, as Scripture and our own standards define it, is more than attendance at worship and a study. A disciple is formed to pray, to be sent, and to reproduce; and that formation is the calling of every member, under the elders, not of the elders alone. Below are the three changes that follow, and the arguments that carry each.
honest_limit: What follows shows what Scripture and our standards require. It does not show what is thin at any particular church. That is something a church can only learn about itself, honestly, by looking.

changes.title: Mission
changes.line: Being sent is inside the definition of a disciple, not a program added to it.
changes.evidence: The strongest case on this page. Carried by precept, by our constitution, and by the Gospels; C4 still stands for an elder who reads Jesus' training of the Twelve as no pattern for a congregation.
changes.verse: Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.

changes.title: Prayer
changes.line: The catechism names three ordinary means, not two. Prayer is the third, and a model built on Word and sacrament has dropped it.
changes.evidence: Made from WSC 88 itself, so it asks nothing beyond our own standards. Scripture fills it in: the one time the disciples asked, in those words, to be taught something, it was prayer.

changes.title: Equipping
changes.line: A disciple is formed to reproduce. Scripture commands formation by watched example, and reports a whole congregation becoming the example to others.
changes.evidence: Well-evidenced, with one caution: the two verses usually quoted for this, Ephesians 4:12 and 2 Timothy 2:2, are the two rated contested. The arguments below carry it more safely.
changes.verse: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.

read_three_why: One from precept, two from our own standards. All three rated firm by the author, all three hold whatever view one takes of Jesus' example, and between them they carry all three changes.

alternative.heading: The other view, fairly stated
alternative.line: Not everyone reads it this way. Some hold that worship, preaching and the sacraments on Sunday are all that the Great Commission asks of a congregation, and that making disciples is the elders' work rather than every member's. Those arguments are here too, made as well as we could make them. Tap any to read it.

common_questions.q: What is the strongest argument that discipleship is more than attendance?
common_questions.a: The summary leads with C4: being sent and reproducing is part of what a disciple is, not an add-on. C3 and C5 make the attendance point directly: the word means an attached learner, and the commands that make up a disciple's life cannot be done from a pew.

common_questions.q: What is the best case that making disciples is the elders' work?
common_questions.a: D1 makes it directly: the ministry of the Word belongs to ordained office, and teaching carries a stricter judgment. C2 and C9 support it from our standards, E3 and G1 from wisdom and history. All five are gathered in the summary under "The other view, fairly stated."

common_questions.q: Does anything here require prayer, or is it a preference?
common_questions.a: C17 rests it on our own standards: WSC 88 and WLC 154 name prayer as one of three ordinary means, with the Word and sacraments. C18 adds the Scripture, starting from Luke 11:1 and Acts 6:4. C16 notes that BCO 8-3 charges elders to pray with and for the people.
Every argument the author rates contested or open is listed here. The summary also states its limit: this shows what Scripture and our standards require, not what is thin at any particular church.

common_questions.q: Which arguments don't need Jesus' example to bind?
common_questions.a: By the author’s tags, these hold on other grounds (a command, our standards, the words themselves), even where they describe what Jesus did. For the narrower question, whether his training of the Twelve is a pattern for a congregation, tick that box on What if.
